# **Live Honeypot**

**Author:** Razin Abbas · **Date:** 2026-11-08 UTC · **Classification:** TLP:AMBER

I created a honeypot in Azure to gain high-fidelity, real-world intelligence on attacker behavior without risking production environments. It is important to note that this honeypot is stationed inside a LogN Pacific managed VNET with its VNET heavily restricting egress traffic. Known abuse ports are denied, and C2 traffic is logged and immediately blocked. This is so our compromised honeypot cannot launch attacks to the rest of our Azure environment or to external targets. This VNET allows all traffic inbound which allows our VM to still be compromised by external threats.

Below is a graph representing the honeypot architecture. We will build the honeypot, add a MySQL DB with dummy data, set up logging to the Microsoft Defender portal , and then write detection rules in Microsoft Sentinel. After capturing a secure baseline, we will expose the device by creating compromised accounts and credentials and disabling all firewalls. We will monitor the device and conduct a full incident response lifecycle after the device is compromised.  
![][image1]

**Building the Honeypot**

A Windows 11 VM named “CRRA-DB-03” was created. Its name implies it contains sensitive information in a DB which encourages it to be targeted. We will create a public IP and attach it to this VMs’ NIC. This public IP is 20.1.204.230. We will subsequently attach a NSG to this device’s NIC to act as a management-plane level firewall for this VM. We will initially block all inbound traffic from the internet on this NSG (default by Inbound Rule 65500\) while we build the honeypot. We will access the VM via Bastion hosts in the same Azure environment. Below is a screenshot of the current state of this NSG.

![][image2]

**SETTING THE STAGE**

We will create a MySQL DB with dummy data to entice discovery (TA0007), collection (TA0009), and exfiltration (TA0010). We will use MySQL Workbench as a GUI to set up this DB. This [script](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1xwJBq_96ehR-obBPZYEgqrSwwmhGSAhW/view?usp=drive_link) was executed which created and populated the following tables: credentials, customers, orders, payments. Below is a screenshot of the created schemas and some instances of the sample data.

![][image3]To enable logging in MySQL, we will run the following script:

**SET GLOBAL general\_log \= 'ON';**

**SET GLOBAL log\_output \= 'FILE';**

**SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'general\_log%';**

We will replace the my.ini file in “C:\\ProgramData\\MySQL\\MySQL Server 8.0\\my.ini” with [my.ini](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1_rc2H24rRgJrN0aQ9m-NLUiR7agcsY2j/view?usp=drive_link). This logs everything to the“mysql\_general.log” file which is located in the same folder and enables network logons which will be used to later expose this DB.

**WIRE LOGGING**

We will now onboard the device to Microsoft Defender for Endpoint via downloading and executing “[Windows 10/11 MDE Package](https://sacyberrange00.blob.core.windows.net/mde-agents/Windows-10-and-11-GatewayWindowsDefenderATPOnboardingPackage.zip)” on the VM. We will validate that MDE is connected  to the Microsoft Defender portal in Azure by checking the “DeviceLogonEvents” table is populated in Advanced Hunting. As shown below, it is populating. 

![][image4]

To wire the MySQL logs in “mysql\_general.log” to Microsoft Defender, we will need to create a Data Collection Rule (DCR) in Microsoft Sentinel. A DCR defines a specific set of logs to be collected on specific Azure resources and sent to specific destinations in Azure. We will be defining a DCR that pulls the logs from the “mysql\_general.log” in the  in “C:\\ProgramData\\MySQL\\MySQL Server 8.0\\” folder in VM “CRRA-DB-03” and sends them to table MySQLAudit\_CL. This table was created by LogN Pacific and is located in Log Analytics Workspaces which is connected to Microsoft Defender, allowing us to query it directly from Defender. Additionally, this DCR will install an agent called “AzureMonitorWindowsAgent” on our VM to extract these logs. The below screenshots show the creation of the DCR and the installation of the agent. 

![][image5]

![][image6]

![][image7]

![][image8]

![][image9]

We can verify the DCR creation and agent installation were successful by querying the mySQLAudit\_CL table in Defender. As shown below, we are getting logs for “CRRA-DB-03” which shows we were successful.

![][image10]

**WRITE DETECTION RULES**

We must now write Sentinel analytic rules that will detect compromise and create incidents in Defender. Our first rule will detect logons to our VM under the “administrator” and “guest” accounts which we will create and make vulnerable later. Below is the Sentinel rule:

**// Virtual Machine Logons**  
**let MyDevice \= "crra-db-03”**  
**DeviceLogonEvents**  
**\| where DeviceName \== MyDevice**  
**\| where AccountName in\~ ("administrator", "guest")**  
**\| where ActionType \== "LogonSuccess"**  
**\| project TimeGenerated, RemoteIP, AccountName, DeviceName, ActionType, LogonType**

We will provide the IP and device name as entity mappings in Sentinel which allows it to automatically extract these fields and conduct incident correlation and trigger automation. In alert metadata, we will map this alert to the following MITRE techniques: Credential Access: Brute Force: Password Guessing (T1110.001) and Initial Access: Valid Accounts: Default Accounts (T1078.001). The below screenshots show the creation of this Sentinel rule. 

![][image11]

![][image12]

![][image13]

![][image14]

We will now create a Sentinel rule to detect a successful login to our MySQL DB after a series of failed logins. The logs from “mysql\_general.log” in MySQLAudit\_CL do not come with the relevant, distinct fields parsed into columns. Instead, there are only two columns: TimeGenerated and RawData with Rawdata which is simply an unorganized dump of various data types. The following detection rule detects a successful breach while parsing out the following columns: DeviceName, ConnectionId, ActionType, Username, and IPAddress and projects it along with TimeGenerated and the original RawData field. 

**// SQL Server \- Failed Login → Successful Login Detection**  
**let MyDevice \= "crra-db-03";**  
**let MyTimeframe \= ago(7d);**  
**let FailedConnections \=**  
    **MySQLAudit\_CL**  
    **\| where TimeGenerated \> MyTimeframe**  
    **\| extend RawData \= replace\_string(RawData, "\\t", " ")**  
    **\| extend DeviceName \= tostring(split(\_ResourceId, "/")\[-1\])**  
    **\| where DeviceName \== MyDevice**  
    **\| where RawData has "Access denied"**  
    **\| extend ConnectionId \= extract(@"^\\S+\\s+(\\d+)\\s+Connect", 1, RawData)**  
    **\| distinct ConnectionId;**  
**MySQLAudit\_CL**  
**\| where TimeGenerated \> MyTimeframe**  
**\| extend RawData \= replace\_string(RawData, "\\t", " ")**  
**\| extend DeviceName \= tostring(split(\_ResourceId, "/")\[-1\])**  
**\| where DeviceName \== MyDevice**  
**\| where RawData has "Connect"**  
**\| extend ConnectionId \= extract(@"^\\S+\\s+(\\d+)\\s+Connect", 1, RawData)**  
**\| extend ActionType \=**  
    **case(**  
        **RawData has "Access denied", "LogonFailure",**  
        **ConnectionId in (FailedConnections), "Ignore",**  
        **"LogonSuccess"**  
    **)**  
**\| where ActionType \!= "Ignore"**  
**\| extend Username \= replace\_string(tostring(split(tostring(split(RawData,"@")\[0\]), " ")\[-1\]), "'", "")**  
**\| extend IpAddress \= replace\_string(tostring(split(split(RawData,"@")\[1\], " ")\[0\]), "'", "")**  
**\| where ActionType \== "LogonSuccess"**  
**\| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, Username, IpAddress, ActionType, RawData**  
**\| order by TimeGenerated desc**

This rule is mapped to Collection: Data from Information Repositories: Databases (T1213.006) and Credential Access: Brute Force: Password Guessing (T1110.001). The entity mapping, alert threshold, and alert grouping fields are identical to the previous Sentinel rule to detect device logons to “CRRA-DB-03.” Below is the creation of this Sentinel rule for the MySQL DB. 

![][image15]

**WEAKEN AND EXPOSE**

Now that our environment is set and our detections in place, we can weaken the machine. We will start by creating two vulnerable accounts. An “administrator” and “Guest” account were created and added to their respective groups in the Computer Management console as shown:

![][image16]![][image17]

The administrator password was set as “password” and the guest password was left blank which makes it so this account does not require a password to be logged on.

In the Local Security Policy console, we will allow the Guest account to logon over the network and locally as this was initially restricted. As shown below, the two policies no longer apply.

![][image18]

Removing a “DENY” is not the same as creating an “ALLOW.” As shown below, we add the Guest account to a policy allowing it to logon via RDP. 

![][image19]

Additionally, there  is a policy that prevents local accounts from logging on with blank passwords. We disabled this so that the Guest can logon.

![][image20]

In RDP settings, we allowed the Guest and administrator accounts to logon remotely as shown:

![][image21]

We will now force the policy to update by running the command shown below. This will force all group policy settings from the domain controller to be applied to “CRRA-DB-03.”

![][image22]

Now that machine is vulnerable, the DB must be made vulnerable as well. A remote user with full root privileges was created. The password for this account was set as “root,” and the account was allowed to be logged onto from anywhere on the network. This was done by running the following query in MySQL:

**CREATE USER 'root'@'%' IDENTIFIED BY 'root';**

**GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON \*.\* TO 'root'@'%' WITH GRANT OPTION;**

**FLUSH PRIVILEGES;**

The entire device is now exposed, but before we completely expose the device to the internet, we must capture a baseline image of the machine. We do this by pulling an investigation package on this device, “CRRA-DB-03” in the Microsoft Defender Portal. 

![][image23]

Now we will expose this device to the internet by disabling Windows Firewall on the endpoint and then updating the NSG on this devices’ NIC to allow inbound traffic from the internet. The below screenshots show Windows Firewall on “CRRA-DB-03” being completely disabled.

![][image24]![][image25]![][image26]

The NSG for this device was updated with the following inbound rule.This rule allows all traffic from anywhere on any port to connect to our VM, making it vulnerable. 

![][image27]

Sep 27, 2026 10:44:14 AM is a timestamp of when the machine was fully vulnerable and exposed. We will use this timestamp to calculate the amount of time it took for “CRRA-DB-03” to get breached.

**DETECT THE BREACH**

At 3:27 PM on Sep 26, 2026, the first alert fired in Microsoft Sentinel for “CRRA-DB-03-MySQL-Logon-Trigger.” The same type of alert fired again at 3:57PM. Later in the day, Sentinel fired two “CRRA-DB-03-Logon-Trigger” alerts at 5:09PM. It took 4 hours and 43 minutes for an alert to fire after we fully exposed this machine. I will now use the following tables to create a timeline of events that led to compromise: DevicLogonEvents, DeviceProcessEvents, DeviceFileEvents, DeviceRegistryEvents, DeviceNetworkEvents, NTANetAnalytics, and MySQLAudit\_CL. I will initially parse through the logs manually to leverage the learning experience I can get from observing a real cyberattack, and will later use the below prompt with Claude to help assist my analysis:

You are a god-tier cybersecurity analyst with world-class threat hunting skills. Please look at these logs, these are \*LOGTYPE\* logs from my environment. Please analyze them and paint a picture of what is going on. 

I will first analyze the MySQL servers’ logons to find out if anyone was able to gain access to it. The below query transforms the MySQLAudit\_CL table to show only failed and successful logons. 

// SQL Server

let MyDevice \= "crra-db-03";

let FailedConnections \=

MySQLAudit\_CL

\| extend RawData \= replace\_string(RawData, "\\t", " ")

\| extend DeviceName \= tostring(split(\_ResourceId, "/")\[-1\])

\| where DeviceName \== MyDevice

\| where RawData has "Access denied"

\| extend ConnectionId \= extract(@"^\\S+\\s+(\\d+)\\s+Connect", 1, RawData)

\| distinct ConnectionId;

MySQLAudit\_CL

\| extend RawData \= replace\_string(RawData, "\\t", " ")

\| extend DeviceName \= tostring(split(\_ResourceId, "/")\[-1\])

\| where DeviceName \== MyDevice

\| where RawData has "Connect"

\| extend ConnectionId \= extract(@"^\\S+\\s+(\\d+)\\s+Connect", 1, RawData)

\| extend ActionType \=

    case(

        RawData has "Access denied", "LogonFailure",

        ConnectionId in (FailedConnections), "Ignore",

        "LogonSuccess"

    )

\| where ActionType \!= "Ignore"

\| extend RawData \= replace\_string(RawData, "\\t", " ")

\| extend Username \= replace\_string(tostring(split(tostring(split(RawData,"@")\[0\]), " ")\[-1\]), "'", "")

\| extend IpAddress \= replace\_string(tostring(split(split(RawData,"@")\[1\], " ")\[0\]), "'", "")

\| where IpAddress \!= "localhost"

\| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, Username, IpAddress, ActionType, RawData

\| order by TimeGenerated desc

There are two IPs, 77.90.185.30 and 45.128.199.183, who were attempting to login to the MySQL server; the same ones flagged in the Sentinel alerts. Both eventually succeeded in logging in as root. Both tried to login in as “admin” and “root” but 77.90.185.30 also attempted to login as “sa” which is the system administrator account for Microsoft SQL. 45.128.199.183 logged in once at 3:49PM but 77.90.185.30 logged in at 3 different times: 3:17PM, 4:39PM, and 5:59PM. 

It is now time to investigate what these two entities did on the MySQL DB. Below is the general KQL query to show all of the MySQL queries made by all IPs. I will later isolate the actions of each IP. 

// Filtering Queries

let MyDevice \= "crra-db-03"; 

MySQLAudit\_CL

\| where RawData has "Query"

\| extend RawData \= replace\_string(RawData, "\\t", " ")

\| extend DeviceName \= tostring(split(\_ResourceId, "/")\[-1\])

\| where DeviceName \== MyDevice

\| extend ActionType \= "Query"

\| extend Query \= split(RawData, "Query")\[1\]

\| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, ActionType, Query, RawData

\| order by TimeGenerated desc

The above query yielded 617 results. I discovered the following through manual analysis:

Various queries like  “SHOW SESSION STATUS LIKE 'Ssl\_cipher'” and “ SHOW SESSION VARIABLES LIKE 'interactive\_timeout'” are run to retrieve details about the configurations of the DB (System Information Discovery: T1082).

Queries like “ SHOW FULL COLUMNS FROM \`crra\_db\_03\`.\`credentials\`” and “ show create table \`orders\`” are used to collect metadata from tables in the DB to figure out what it contains, how tables were created, and their relationship to other tables (Collection: T1213.006).

Queries like “ SHOW TRIGGERS LIKE 'customers'” are used to find out if actions committed against the DB will result in actions that can harm the attackers’ goal.

“ CREATE TABLE \`crra\_db\_03\`.\`RECOVER\_YOUR\_DATA\_info\` (\`READ\_ME\` text) ENGINE=InnoDB DEFAULT CHARSET=utf8” and “ INSERT INTO \`crra\_db\_03\`.\`RECOVER\_YOUR\_DATA\_info\` (\`READ\_ME\`) VALUES ('Saved file name: crra\_db\_03.sql” confirms that the DB has suffered a ransomware attack (T1657).

After the ransomware information was inserted into the DB, every single table was dropped (T1485). This makes sense as the attacker wants us to pay a ransom to recover our tables. It is important to note 617 queries were executed in just 2 minutes which means this ransomware attack was conducted by a bot. It is important to note the main ransomware attack and 614 out of 617 queries was conducted by 45.128.199.183 and 77.90.185.30 only pushed 3 queries to discover the configurations of the DB.

I will now leverage the power of LLMs to conduct big data analysis on the logs since there is a chance I may have missed something important due to the large amount of logs. The below command was ran:

You are a god-tier cybersecurity analyst with world-class threat hunting skills. Please look at these logs, these are MySQL audit logs from my environment. Please analyze them and paint a picture of what is going on. 

Below is the executive summary Claude provided:

“This is a complete, automated MySQL ransom-and-wipe attack, executed start-to-finish in 83 seconds (15:49:08–15:50:31 UTC, Sep 27). The attacker connected as root, systematically dumped every database on the server, dropped every table in each one, and left a ransom note in each database claiming the data was "saved” and demanding payment for its return.”

In the analysis provided, Claude corroborates my analysis but also provides missed but relevant information. Claude mentioned how the attacker first locked all of my DBs before dumping them and how ransom notes were also added to the default MySQL tables located in the same MySQL environment. I logged onto “CRRA-DB-03” and pulled the ransom note: “All your data was backed up by us. You must pay 0.0101 bitcoin to bc1qt6kstjjdatqnxd3ksdcfv0jnhdjzndcnkx8zla or in 48 hours, your data will be publicly disclosed and deleted. (for more information visit https\://cuq.in/844) After payment send mail to ak+2xopd@onionmail.org and we will provide a link for you to download your data. Your DATAID is: 2XOPD”

I will now investigate DeviceLogonEvents to understand who logged into CRRA-DB-03. I will use the below KQL query:

// Virtual Machine Logons  
let MyDevice \= "crra-db-03";  
DeviceLogonEvents  
\| where DeviceName \== MyDevice  
\| where AccountName in\~ ("administrator", "guest")  
\| project TimeGenerated, RemoteIP, AccountName, DeviceName, ActionType, LogonType  
\| order by TimeGenerated desc

The VM was finally breached on Oct 8, 2026 at 3:18:43 PM. The reason it took almost 2 weeks for a full breach was because I had made a major misconfiguration to the account lockout policies. ELABORATE AND ADD SC

Two IPs logged into the “administrator” account within 2 minutes of each other. 223.26.63.26, a Hong Kong IP, logged in on Oct 8, 2026 at 3:18:43 PM. Shortly after, 171.253.171.91, a Vietnamese IP, logged in on Oct 8, 2026 at 3:19:51 PM. It is important to note that the Hong Kong IP was flagged by one vendor as  malicious in Virutotal while the other has nothing. Since we don’t know if both IPs were logged in at the same time or whether one took priority over the other, we must also project “InitiatingProcessRemoteSessionIP” when investigating DeviceProcessEvents and DeviceFileEvents. 

Here is the primary query to check the DeviceLogonEvents table:

let MyDevice \= "crra-db-03";

DeviceProcessEvents

\| where DeviceName \== MyDevice

\| where TimeGenerated \>= datetime(2026-10-08 15:18:43)

\| where InitiatingProcessAccountName \== "administrator"

\| project TimeGenerated, ActionType, FileName, InitiatingProcessRemoteSessionIP, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, AccountName

\| sort by TimeGenerated desc

This is the query to investigate DeviceProcessEvents:

let MyDevice \= "crra-db-03";

DeviceProcessEvents

\| where DeviceName \== MyDevice

\| where TimeGenerated \>= datetime(2026-10-08 15:18:43)

\| where InitiatingProcessAccountName \== "administrator"

\| project TimeGenerated, ActionType, FileName, InitiatingProcessRemoteSessionIP, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, AccountName

\| sort by TimeGenerated desc

This is the query to investigate DeviceFileEvents:

let MyDevice \= "crra-db-03";

DeviceFileEvents

\| where DeviceName \== MyDevice

\| where Timestamp \>= datetime(2026-10-08 15:18:43)

\| where InitiatingProcessAccountName \=="administrator"

\| project Timestamp, ActionType, FileName,  FolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessRemoteSessionIP, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileOriginUrl, FileOriginIP

\| sort by Timestamp desc

I spent countless hours of screentime trying to understand the results of this query, including consulting with Claude. After understanding what normal looks like and some indicators to gauge whether activity was automatically done by Windows or Azure, I felt comfortable writing this report (go into this more later)

I will go through the logs manually to get a summary of the events that happened and use Claude to do the full detailed investigation with collectables. “mimkatz.exe,” a security tool used to extract critical information from Windows system memory, and “svchost.com,” a program masquerading as the legitimate Windows binary “svchost.exe” were used to stage a complex crypto-mining cyberattack. After checking "Task Manager” and “Local Users and Groups” in “Computer Management,” the attacker launched “mimikatz.exe” and “[svchost.com](http://svchost.com).” “[svchost.com](http://svchost.com)” was interacted with by the GUI (explorer.exe) and launched “msedge.exe” to conduct actions in the Edge web browser. Eventually, “cookie\_exporter.exe” was launched from Edge. A temporary file called “5jPB8sPc.exe” was created and deleted during this process in the “C:\\Users\\administrator\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\” folder. A file called “1.txt” was created in the “C:\\Users\\administrator\\Documents\\mimikatz\\mimikatz\\” folder by process “\_CACHE\~1.EXE” which was a child process of “mimikatz.exe.” Two different Chrome extensions were downloaded into Edge and multiple files were modified in the “C:\\Users\\administrator\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\scoped\_dir7928\_583634239\\CRX\_INSTALL\\” and “VC:\\Users\\administrator\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\scoped\_dir7928\_242738888\\CRX\_INSTALL\\” folders. Eventually “SRBMiner-Multi-0-7-7,” a cryptominer was launched from the GUI (explorer.exe) and multiple files were created in the “C:\\Users\\administrator\\Desktop\\SRBMiner-Multi-0-7-7\\guided-setup.bat” folder including a file called “ReadMe.txt.” At the end of the attack, “SRBMiner-MULTI.exe” was deleted from the system within a minute, likely by antivirus. Based on my current manual analysis, I cannot pinpoint how SRBMiner, mimikatz, and cookieexporter, and svchost.com were downloaded onto the machine. I will now consult Claude. 

The following Claude prompt was used to analyze the DeviceFileEvents and DeviceProcessEvents tables: 

“You are a god-tier cybersecurity analyst with world-class threat hunting skills.

Please look at these logs, these are Microsoft Defender (MDE) logs from my environment.

Please analyze them and paint a picture for what might be going on.”

I used Claude Opus 5.5 at Medium effort for my investigation. 

Claude pointed out to me that at “3:21:37 PM: windowsdefender://threat was opened. This is the Defender protection page, and it usually means someone is checking for or disabling protection.” This is something that I completely missed. It pointed out that the files that were downloaded to and launched from my device where likely RDP copy-paste files. This explains how the files in question got onto my device.  Additionally, it asked me to check the DeviceRegistryEvents table for any registry modifications. I used the below query to check it: 

let MyDevice \= "crra-db-03";

DeviceRegistryEvents

\| where DeviceName \== MyDevice

\| where Timestamp \>= datetime(2026-10-08 15:18:43)

\| where InitiatingProcessAccountName \=="administrator"

\| project Timestamp, ActionType, RegistryValueData, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName ,  InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessRemoteSessionIP, InitiatingProcessAccountName

\| sort by Timestamp desc

After pasting the results into Claude, I discovered that the hijacker established persistence by modifying the Registry. They made it so that every “.exe” file would be executed by the malicious “svchost.com” and not “svchost.exe” as indicated by key “HKLM\\SOFTWARE\\Classes\\exefile\\shell\\open\\command” being set to value “C:\\Windows\\svchost.com "%1" %\*.”The attacker goes on to establish persistence by forcing the “Synaptics Pointing Device Driver” in “HKLM\\SOFTWARE\\WOW6432Node\\Microsoft\\Windows\\CurrentVersion\\Run” (the Windows Run Key) to point to “C:\\ProgramData\\Synaptics\\Synaptics.exe.” The binary at this path is a malicious executable mimicking a real Windows process located in “ProgramData” instead of “System32” where the real executable is located. It's also important to note that “mimikatz.exe” initiated the process that modified this registry value. I revisited the DeviceFileEvents table and confirmed that “Synaptics.exe” in folder “C:\\ProgramData\\Synaptics\\Synaptics.exe” was one of the many files created by “mimikatz.exe” during this attack. 

Unfortunately, I could not capture the investigation package and do a manual analysis of “CRRA-DB-03” by logging into the device as “administrator” because I went on vacation and LogN Pacific automation deleted my entire VM. I will continue to do honeypots like this in the future so this will not be an issue. If this did not happen, I would isolate the device in Defender to contain the breach and then capture an investigation package. I would then move onto eradication and recovery.

In order to eradicate the threat, I would reimage the VM from a known good image prior to the attack, enable Windows Firewall, harden to NSG to implement least privilege, delete the administrator account, disable the guest account, disable logging onto the MySQL DB from the internet, run a Defender AV scan, and finally remove the device from isolation.
